title: First Microblazar Found in Milky Way: Black Hole Jet Aimed at Earth
excerpt: IRAS 18293−0941, a stellar-mass black hole 12,000 light-years away firing plasma at 75% light speed toward Earth, is the first confirmed microblazar — and a 100-times-more-powerful natural accelerator than the LHC.
body:
• The discovery: An international team led by ASTRON, JIVE and the University of Amsterdam has identified IRAS 18293−0941, about 12,000 light-years away, as the first confirmed microblazar in the Milky Way — a stellar-mass black hole firing a jet of plasma almost directly at Earth. The paper, accepted by Astronomy & Astrophysics, was announced September 22, 2026.
  • What a microblazar is: The small-scale cousin of blazars — supermassive black holes at the centers of distant galaxies whose jets happen to point at us. Here, the "engine" is a black hole just 10 times the Sun's mass, orbiting a hot massive star every 11.38 days and stripping matter from it.
  • The extreme physics: The jet travels at 75% the speed of light. The opposite jet smashes into a molecular cloud 100 light-years away, accelerating particles to peta-electronvolt energies — making this object about 100 times more powerful than the Large Hadron Collider.
  • Is it dangerous? No. At 12,000 light-years, the jet poses no threat to Earth. What it offers instead is a nearby laboratory: distant blazars are too far to image in detail, but this one sits in our own galaxy.

Somewhere in the constellation Scutum, about 12,000 light-years away, a black hole is firing a jet of near-light-speed plasma almost directly at Earth — and astronomers only just noticed. The object, known as IRAS 18293−0941, has been catalogued since 1983 and then largely forgotten. On September 22, an international team announced that it is the first confirmed microblazar in the Milky Way, ending a search that began roughly thirty years ago when theorists predicted such objects must exist.

The discovery paper, led by researchers at ASTRON, JIVE (the Joint Institute for VLBI in Europe) and the University of Amsterdam, has been accepted by the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics. The team pre-published the work on arXiv on September 1, drawing on radio observations from the European VLBI Network and the MeerKAT array in South Africa, plus positional data from the European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft.

Context & Background

To understand the find, start with blazars. Across the universe, supermassive black holes — millions or billions of times the Sun's mass — sit at the centers of galaxies, devouring surrounding matter. Some of that matter gets funneled out along the black hole's poles as twin jets of plasma and radiation traveling near light speed. When one of those jets happens to point at Earth, the object looks dramatically brighter because the jet's motion beams its radiation toward us. That's a blazar.

A microblazar is the same physics at a vastly smaller scale: instead of a galactic monster, the engine is a stellar-mass black hole. Theorists have argued for decades that our galaxy should contain such systems, but none had been confirmed — partly because they're hard to see. IRAS 18293−0941 sits behind a thick wall of interstellar gas and dust, invisible to ordinary optical telescopes.

"It sits behind so much dust that it is essentially invisible in ordinary optical images. It was catalogued decades ago and then more or less forgotten."

— Josep Martí, University of Jaén

The giveaway was a flicker. Researchers noticed the companion star's light pulsing on an 11.38-day rhythm — the orbital period of the black hole around it — which told them they were viewing the system nearly face-on, with the jet pointed at them. European VLBI Network imaging then showed a bright central source with a one-sided structure: one jet visible, the other hidden. By combining the radio images with Gaia astrometry, Benito Marcote of JIVE confirmed the jet belonged to the local binary system and ruled out a background galaxy. "Everything about IRAS 18293−0941 was hiding in plain sight," team leader Roi Rahin of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County and NASA Goddard Space Flight Center said in a statement.

Impact & Analysis

The science payoff comes from the far end of the system. While the Earth-facing jet brightens the object through Doppler boosting, the opposite jet — pointed away from us — traverses about 100 light-years of space the system has already cleared of interstellar medium, then collides with a dense molecular cloud of hydrogen and dust. That collision creates a glowing hotspot where interstellar material is ionized and dust is heated, and it accelerates particles to nearly light speed at energies in the peta-electronvolt range.

The hotspot coincides with LHAASO J1831-1007u, a source of ultra-high-energy gamma rays detected by China's Large High Altitude Air Shower Observatory. That match suggests microblazars may be one of the long-sought sources of the most energetic cosmic rays in the galaxy — the particles researchers call PeVatrons. The energies involved make the microblazar one of the most powerful natural particle accelerators in the Milky Way, roughly 100 times more powerful than CERN's Large Hadron Collider, humanity's most powerful machine.

"Thanks to this discovery, we can study distant blazars, which are formed by distant supermassive black holes. Those blazars are too far away to image in detail. Because we now have a similar object in our own galaxy, we can study its physics in detail."

— Benito Marcote, ASTRON and JIVE

For particle physics, that matters because no Earth-based machine can reach peta-electronvolt energies. The universe is running the experiments; astronomers are only now learning where to look.

Diaspora Angle

The Indian connection runs through the instruments rather than the object itself. South Africa's MeerKAT — whose radio images were central to confirming the counter-jet hotspot — shares skies and survey strategies with the Giant Metrewave Radio Telescope near Pune, and Indian radio astronomers have long contributed to multi-observatory campaigns like this one. The microblazar result itself is pure blue-sky astrophysics: a reminder that the night sky above India and above the diaspora holds the same 12,000-light-year mystery.

What's Next

The team expects the newly confirmed microblazar to become a workhorse object for high-energy astrophysics — a nearby stand-in for distant blazars that can't be resolved in detail. Open questions remain: how many more microblazars are hiding behind dust elsewhere in the galaxy, and how much of the Milky Way's most energetic cosmic radiation they account for. With the hotspot's gamma-ray signature now mapped, astronomers know exactly where to point next.
